claim: Mammalian olfaction and reproduction are tightly linked.
source: Mammalian olfaction and reproduction are tightly linked, a link less explored in humans.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature on the topic

claim: Most women with uRPL could identify the body-odor of their spouse.
source: We found that whereas most women with uRPL could identify the body-odor of their spouse, most control women could not.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the spouse identification task

claim: Most control women could not identify the body-odor of their spouse.
source: We found that whereas most women with uRPL could identify the body-odor of their spouse, most control women could not.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the spouse identification task

claim: Women with uRPL rated the perceptual attributes of men's body-odor differently from controls.
source: Moreover, women with uRPL rated the perceptual attributes of men's body-odor differently from controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from body-odor rating tasks

claim: Women with uRPL have a modest but significant advantage in ordinary, non-body-odor-related olfaction.
source: These pronounced differences were accompanied by an only modest albeit significant advantage in ordinary, non-body-odor-related olfaction in uRPL.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from olfactory identification, discrimination, and detection tasks

claim: Most women with uRPL had smaller olfactory bulbs compared to controls.
source: Next, using structural and functional brain imaging, we found that in comparison to controls, most women with uRPL had smaller olfactory bulbs, yet increased hypothalamic response in association with men's body-odor.
evidence: Supported by structural MRI measurements of olfactory bulb volume

claim: Women with uRPL had increased hypothalamic response in association with men's body-odor.
source: Next, using structural and functional brain imaging, we found that in comparison to controls, most women with uRPL had smaller olfactory bulbs, yet increased hypothalamic response in association with men's body-odor.
evidence: Supported by functional MRI data during body-odor exposure

claim: Body-odors from adult males can lead to accelerated pubertal development in juvenile female rodents.
source: This link has been extensively studied in rodents, where body-odors from adult males can lead to accelerated pubertal development in juvenile females (Vandenbergh, 1967), to synchronous estrous cycling in adult females (Whitten, 1956; Whitten, 1958), and to implantation failure (Bruce, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vandenbergh, 1967

claim: Body-odors from adult males can lead to synchronous estrous cycling in adult female rodents.
source: This link has been extensively studied in rodents, where body-odors from adult males can lead to accelerated pubertal development in juvenile females (Vandenbergh, 1967), to synchronous estrous cycling in adult females (Whitten, 1956; Whitten, 1958), and to implantation failure (Bruce, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citations to Whitten, 1956 and Whitten, 1958

claim: Body-odors from adult males can lead to implantation failure in female rodents.
source: This link has been extensively studied in rodents, where body-odors from adult males can lead to accelerated pubertal development in juvenile females (Vandenbergh, 1967), to synchronous estrous cycling in adult females (Whitten, 1956; Whitten, 1958), and to implantation failure (Bruce, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruce, 1959

claim: Social odors in rodents are typically transduced at the vomeronasal organ in the nose.
source: Such social odors are typically transduced at the vomeronasal organ in the nose, and processed through the accessory olfactory system in the brain (Dulac, 2000; Luo and Katz, 2004), but there is also evidence for reproductive social odors acting through the main olfactory system as well (Kang et al., 2009; Baum and Cherry, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dulac, 2000 and Luo and Katz, 2004

claim: Social odors in rodents are processed through the accessory olfactory system in the brain.
source: Such social odors are typically transduced at the vomeronasal organ in the nose, and processed through the accessory olfactory system in the brain (Dulac, 2000; Luo and Katz, 2004), but there is also evidence for reproductive social odors acting through the main olfactory system as well (Kang et al., 2009; Baum and Cherry, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dulac, 2000 and Luo and Katz, 2004

claim: There is evidence for reproductive social odors acting through the main olfactory system in rodents.
source: Such social odors are typically transduced at the vomeronasal organ in the nose, and processed through the accessory olfactory system in the brain (Dulac, 2000; Luo and Katz, 2004), but there is also evidence for reproductive social odors acting through the main olfactory system as well (Kang et al., 2009; Baum and Cherry, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Baum and Cherry, 2015

claim: Women who cohabitate tend to have a synchronized menstrual cycle.
source: Here, women who cohabitate tend to have a synchronized menstrual cycle (McClintock, 1971), an effect mediated by women's body-odor (Stern and McClintock, 1998) (this effect has been challenged on statistical grounds (Strassmann, 1999), yet our view is that it holds).
evidence: Supported by citation to McClintock, 1971

claim: Menstrual synchrony is mediated by women's body-odor.
source: Here, women who cohabitate tend to have a synchronized menstrual cycle (McClintock, 1971), an effect mediated by women's body-odor (Stern and McClintock, 1998) (this effect has been challenged on statistical grounds (Strassmann, 1999), yet our view is that it holds).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stern and McClintock, 1998

claim: Body-odor from breast-feeding women timed ovulation and menstruation in nulliparous women.
source: In a different set of related studies, the body-odor from breast-feeding women timed ovulation and menstruation in nulliparous women (Jacob et al., 2004), and increased their sexual motivation (Spencer et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacob et al., 2004

claim: Body-odor from breast-feeding women increased sexual motivation in nulliparous women.
source: In a different set of related studies, the body-odor from breast-feeding women timed ovulation and menstruation in nulliparous women (Jacob et al., 2004), and increased their sexual motivation (Spencer et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spencer et al., 2004

claim: Men's body-odors were found to regulate menstrual cycle variability in women.
source: In turn, men's body-odors were found to regulate menstrual cycle variability in women (Cutler et al., 1986; Preti et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cutler et al., 1986 and Preti et al., 2003

claim: Women's preference for men's body-odors are menstrual cycle phase-dependent.
source: This is consistent with findings implying that women's preference for men's body-odors are menstrual cycle phase-dependent (Havlicek et al., 2005; Rantala et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Havlicek et al., 2005 and Rantala et al., 2006

claim: Maternal status was found to regulate neural responses to the body-odor of newborns.
source: Moreover, maternal status was found to regulate neural responses to the body-odor of newborns (Lundström et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lundström et al., 2013

claim: Men rate women's axillary and vaginal odors as most pleasant around ovulation.
source: For example, attractiveness ratings applied by men to women's body-odors are menstrual-phase specific (Kuukasjarvi, 2004), with men rating women's axillary and vaginal odors as most pleasant around ovulation (Doty et al., 1975; Singh and Bronstad, 2001; Gildersleeve et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doty et al., 1975, Singh and Bronstad, 2001, and Gildersleeve et al., 2012

claim: Sniffing emotional tears collected from women donors reduced levels of testosterone in men.
source: In addition, sniffing emotional tears collected from women donors reduced levels of testosterone (Gelstein et al., 2011; Oh et al., 2012) and ensuing arousal in men (Gelstein et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gelstein et al., 2011 and Oh et al., 2012

claim: Sniffing emotional tears collected from women donors reduced arousal in men.
source: In addition, sniffing emotional tears collected from women donors reduced levels of testosterone (Gelstein et al., 2011; Oh et al., 2012) and ensuing arousal in men (Gelstein et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gelstein et al., 2011

claim: Approximately 50% of all human conceptions end in spontaneous miscarriage.
source: A remarkable ~50% of all human conceptions, and ~15% of documented human pregnancies, end in spontaneous miscarriage (Rai and Regan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rai and Regan, 2006

claim: Approximately 15% of documented human pregnancies end in spontaneous miscarriage.
source: A remarkable ~50% of all human conceptions, and ~15% of documented human pregnancies, end in spontaneous miscarriage (Rai and Regan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rai and Regan, 2006

claim: Only a limited portion of miscarriages can be explained.
source: Only a limited portion of these miscarriages, however, can be explained (Clifford et al., 1994; Stephenson, 1996; Jaslow et al., 2010), suggesting the presence of major yet-unidentified human-miscarriage-related factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Clifford et al., 1994, Stephenson, 1996, and Jaslow et al., 2010

claim: The study tested 33 women with uRPL with a mean age of 34.7 ± 6.4 and mean number of miscarriages of 4.2.
source: To characterize olfactory spouse-recognition in humans, we tested 33 women with uRPL (mean age = 34.7 ± 6.4, mean number of miscarriages = 4.2) and 33 matched controls (mean age = 35.6 ± 4.1, never experienced miscarriage).
evidence: Supported by experimental data describing the participant cohort

claim: The study tested 33 matched controls with a mean age of 35.6 ± 4.1 who never experienced miscarriage.
source: To characterize olfactory spouse-recognition in humans, we tested 33 women with uRPL (mean age = 34.7 ± 6.4, mean number of miscarriages = 4.2) and 33 matched controls (mean age = 35.6 ± 4.1, never experienced miscarriage).
evidence: Supported by experimental data describing the participant cohort

claim: Control women were unable to identify their spouse above chance levels (mean control = 28 ± 34%).
source: Here, consistent with the two former studies, as a group, control women were unable to identify their spouse above chance levels (chance = 33.3%, mean control = 28 ± 34%, Shapiro-Wilk test of normality (SW) = 0.77, p<0.001, difference from chance: Wilcoxon W = 206, p=0.18, effect size estimated by rank biserial correlation (RBC) = 1.17 (parametric comparison: t(32) = 0.88, p=0.39, Cohen's d = 0.15)).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the spouse identification task with statistical analysis

claim: uRPL women were able to identify their spouse by body-odor alone at a level significantly higher than expected by chance (mean uRPL = 57 ± 41%).
source: In contrast, remarkably, uRPL women were able to identify their spouse by body-odor alone, at a level that was both significantly higher than expected by chance (chance = 33.3%, mean uRPL = 57 ± 41%, SW = 0.81, p<0.001), difference from chance: Wilcoxon W = 440, p=0.004, RBC = 1.71 (parametric comparison: t(32) = 3.32, p=0.002, Cohen's d = 0.58), and two-fold that of controls (Mann-Whitney U = 332.5, p=0.005, RBC = 0.39, parametric comparison: t(64) = 3.12, p=0.003, Cohen's d = 0.77) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the spouse identification task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1b

claim: uRPL women's spouse identification performance was two-fold that of controls.
source: In contrast, remarkably, uRPL women were able to identify their spouse by body-odor alone, at a level that was both significantly higher than expected by chance (chance = 33.3%, mean uRPL = 57 ± 41%, SW = 0.81, p<0.001), difference from chance: Wilcoxon W = 440, p=0.004, RBC = 1.71 (parametric comparison: t(32) = 3.32, p=0.002, Cohen's d = 0.58), and two-fold that of controls (Mann-Whitney U = 332.5, p=0.005, RBC = 0.39, parametric comparison: t(64) = 3.12, p=0.003, Cohen's d = 0.77) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the spouse identification task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1b

claim: The probability of obtaining the spouse identification results coincidentally is 2 in 1000.
source: We observe that the probability of obtaining our results coincidentally is 2 in 1000, further suggesting that this result was not a chance event (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 1c

claim: There was only a trend toward better identification in uRPL women than in controls for ordinary odor identification (mean uRPL = 87.6% ± 7.2, Controls = 84.6% ± 7.3).
source: We observed only a trend toward better identification in uRPL women than in controls (mean uRPL = 87.6% ± 7.2, Controls = 84.6% ± 7.3, uRPL SW = 0.91, p=0.005, control SW = 0.92, p=0.009, Mann-Whitney U = 560.5, p=0.087, RBC = 0.22 (parametric comparison: t(74) = 1.82, p=0.073, Cohen's d = 0.42)) (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the odor identification task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2a

claim: At fixed concentrations, EST was harder to detect than both AND and ANN (mean EST = 41.8 ± 29.4, mean AND = 58.1 ± 34.6, mean ANN = 66.2 ± 31).
source: The main effect of Odorant reflected that at these particular concentrations, EST was harder to detect than both AND and ANN (mean EST = 41.8 ± 29.4, mean AND = 58.1 ± 34.6, mean ANN = 66.2 ± 31: AND vs. ANN Wilcoxon W = 858, p=0.068, RBC = 0.29 (parametric comparison: t(70) = 1.7, p=0.093, Cohen's d = 0.2); AND vs EST Wilcoxon W = 451, p=6.4e−4, RBC = 0.51 (parametric comparison: t(70) = 3.5, p=8.2e-4, Cohen's d = 0.42); ANN vs. EST: Wilcoxon W = 237, p=6e−7, RBC = 0.74 (parametric comparison: t(75) = 5.86, p=1.2e−7, Cohen's d = 0.67) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the monomolecule discrimination task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2b

claim: There was no significant difference between controls and uRPL in detection threshold for DMTS (uRPL threshold: 4.98 ± 0.41, control threshold: 5.06 ± 0.72).
source: We observed no significant difference between controls and uRPL (uRPL threshold, minus log concentration: 4.98 ± 0.41, control threshold: 5.06 ± 0.72, uRPL SW = 0.92, p=0.13, control SW = 0.9, p=0.052, t(34) = 0.42, p=0.68, Cohen's d = 0.14) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the DMTS threshold task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2c

claim: There was a small but significant difference between uRPL and controls in composite olfaction score (mean composite uRPL = 57.13% ± 15.23, Controls = 49.46% ± 16.14).
source: We observed a small but significant difference between the two groups (mean composite uRPL = 57.13% ± 15.23, Controls = 49.46% ± 16.14, uRPL SW = 0.97, p=0.49, control SW = 0.98, p=0.67, independent t-test t(76) = 2.16, p=0.034, Cohen's d = 0.49) (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the composite olfaction score with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2d

claim: The probability of obtaining the composite olfaction score result by chance is less than 2 in 100.
source: To verify that this was not a chance event, we again conducted a 10,000-repetion bootstrap like before, and observe that the probability of obtaining this result by chance is less than 2 in 100 (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 2e

claim: uRPL and Control women rated Blank and Spouse body-odors the same.
source: As to the Odor x Group interaction, whereas uRPL and Control women rated Blank and Spouse the same (uRPL Blank:=0.36 ± 0.2; Control Blank:=0.39 ± 0.18, Mann-Whitney U = 173, p=0.74, RBC = 0.07 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 0.49, p=0.63, Cohen's d = 0.16); uRPL Spouse = 0.46 ± 0.23; Control Spouse = 0.37 ± 0.21, Mann- Whitney U = 121, p = 0.2, RBC = 0.25 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 1.25, p=0.22, Cohen's d = 0.42), Non-Spouse was rated lower by uRPL than by Controls (uRPL = 0.36 ± 0.18; Controls = 0.49 ± 0.14, Mann-Whitney U = 244, p=0.009, RBC = 0.51 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 2.35, p=0.025, Cohen's d = 0.78) (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the body-odor rating task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3a

claim: Non-Spouse body-odor was rated lower by uRPL than by Controls (uRPL = 0.36 ± 0.18; Controls = 0.49 ± 0.14).
source: As to the Odor x Group interaction, whereas uRPL and Control women rated Blank and Spouse the same (uRPL Blank:=0.36 ± 0.2; Control Blank:=0.39 ± 0.18, Mann-Whitney U = 173, p=0.74, RBC = 0.07 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 0.49, p=0.63, Cohen's d = 0.16); uRPL Spouse = 0.46 ± 0.23; Control Spouse = 0.37 ± 0.21, Mann- Whitney U = 121, p = 0.2, RBC = 0.25 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 1.25, p=0.22, Cohen's d = 0.42), Non-Spouse was rated lower by uRPL than by Controls (uRPL = 0.36 ± 0.18; Controls = 0.49 ± 0.14, Mann-Whitney U = 244, p=0.009, RBC = 0.51 (parametric comparison: t(34) = 2.35, p=0.025, Cohen's d = 0.78) (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the body-odor rating task with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3a

claim: The probability of obtaining the non-spouse body-odor rating result by chance is less than 6 in 1000.
source: Again, to verify that this result with non-spouse odors was not a chance event, we conducted a 10,000-repetion bootstrap like before, and observe that the probability of obtaining this result by chance is less than 6 in 1000 (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: Women with uRPL have significantly smaller olfactory bulbs (Right bulb volume: uRPL: 45.9 ± 12 mm3, control: 55.4 ± 9.7 mm3; Left bulb volume: uRPL: 46.4 ± 8.9 mm3, control: 55.7 ± 9.4 mm3; Average bulb volume: uRPL: 46.1 ± 9.9 mm3, control: 55.5 ± 9 mm3).
source: We observed that women with uRPL have significantly smaller olfactory bulbs (all SW >0.94, all p>0.2; Right bulb volume: uRPL: 45.9 ± 12 mm3, control: 55.4 ± 9.7 mm3, t(44) = 2.96, p=0.005, Cohen's d = 0.87; Left bulb volume: uRPL: 46.4 ± 8.9 mm3, control: 55.7 ± 9.4 mm3, t(44) = 3.45, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 1.02; Average bulb volume: uRPL: 46.1 ± 9.9 mm3, control: 55.5 ± 9 mm3, t(44) = 3.37, p=0.0016, Cohen's d = 0.99) (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by structural MRI measurements with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4a

claim: The probability of obtaining the olfactory bulb volume result by chance is less than 1 in 1000.
source: To verify that this was not a chance event, we again conducted a 10,000-repetion bootstrap like before, and observe that the probability of obtaining this result by chance is less than 1 in 1000 (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4b

claim: Women with uRPL had significantly shallower olfactory sulci (Left olfactory sulcus depth: uRPL: 6.1 ± 1.4 mm, control: 7 ± 1.4 mm; Average olfactory sulcus depth: uRPL: 6.3 ± 1.1 mm, control: 7 ± 1.3 mm).
source: Women with uRPL also had significantly shallower olfactory sulci (Right olfactory sulcus depth did not reach significance: uRPL: 6.4 ± 1.1 mm, control: 7.1 ± 1.4 mm, t(44) = 1.68, p=0.1, Cohen's d = 0.5; Left olfactory sulcus depth: uRPL: 6.1 ± 1.4 mm, control: 7 ± 1.4 mm, t(44) = 2.22, p=0.03, Cohen's d = 0.66; Average olfactory sulcus depth: uRPL: 6.3 ± 1.1 mm, control: 7 ± 1.3 mm, t(44) = 2.12, p=0.04, Cohen's d = 0.62) (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by structural MRI measurements with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4c

claim: The probability of obtaining the olfactory sulcus depth result by chance is less than 2 in 100.
source: To verify that this was not a chance event, we again conducted a 10,000-repetion bootstrap like before, and observe that the probability of obtaining this result by chance is less than 2 in 100 (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4d

claim: There was no difference in Total Intracranial Volume between uRPL women and controls (TIV: uRPL mean: 1366 ± 134 cm3, Control mean: 1390 ± 93 cm3).
source: To verify that these anatomical differences were not merely a reflection of smaller heads/brains, we conducted the same analysis on Total Intracranial Volume (TIV), and observe no difference between uRPL women and controls (TIV: uRPL mean: 1366 ± 134 cm3, Control mean: 1390 ± 93 cm3, uRPL SW = 0.95, p=0.31, control SW = 0.94, p=0.2, t(43) = 0.69, p=0.5, Cohen's d = 0.21).
evidence: Supported by structural MRI measurements with statistical analysis

claim: There was a significant correlation between olfaction composite score and olfactory bulb volume in the uRPL cohort alone (uRPL: n = 22, Spearman Rho = 0.45, p=0.037).
source: Using this more comprehensive olfactory score, we observed a significant correlation in the uRPL cohort alone (uRPL: n = 22, Spearman Rho = 0.45, p=0.037; Control: n = 23, Spearman Rho = −0.055, p=0.8; Combined: n = 45, Spearman Rho = 0.065, p=0.67) (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4e

claim: Body-odor increased hypothalamic activation in uRPL women.
source: We observed that whereas body-odor increased hypothalamic activation in uRPL (t(22) = 2.81, p=0.01), it decreased hypothalamic activation in controls (t(22) = 2.41, p=0.025), and the interaction was powerful (F(1,44) = 13.4, p=0.0007) (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by functional MRI data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5a

claim: Body-odor decreased hypothalamic activation in control women.
source: We observed that whereas body-odor increased hypothalamic activation in uRPL (t(22) = 2.81, p=0.01), it decreased hypothalamic activation in controls (t(22) = 2.41, p=0.025), and the interaction was powerful (F(1,44) = 13.4, p=0.0007) (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by functional MRI data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5a

claim: With increased arousal, body-odor increased connectivity between the hypothalamus and right insula significantly more in controls than in uRPL.
source: We observed that with increased arousal, body-odor increased connectivity between the hypothalamus and right insula significantly more in controls than in uRPL (peak Montreal Neurological Institute coordinates (MNI): [33,21,-8], 2336 voxels, Cluster-corrected z > 3.1) (Figure 5b)
evidence: Supported by functional MRI PPI analysis and shown in Figure 5b

claim: Both uRPL and controls had moderate anxiety levels with no significant difference between the groups (STAI: uRPL = 39.5 ± 8, Control = 39.87 ± 10.86).
source: We observed that both uRPL and controls had moderate anxiety levels, and there was no significant difference between the groups (STAI: uRPL = 39.5 ± 8, Control = 39.87 ± 10.86, SW = 0.97, p=0.3, t(44) = 0.14, p=0.89, Cohen's d = 0.041).
evidence: Supported by questionnaire data with statistical analysis

claim: There were no significant differences in personality between uRPL and control groups.
source: Moreover, we observed no significant differences in personality (Extroversion (E), Conscientiousness (C), Neuroticism (N) Agreeableness (A), Openness to experience (O)); uRPL: E = 3.67 ± 0.59, C = 3.71 ± 0.49, N = 3.05 ± 0.67, A = 3.87 ± 0.46, O = 3.58 ± 0.67. Control: E = 3.51 ± 0.64, C = 3.94 ± 0.41, N = 2.97 ± 0.65, A = 3.73 ± 0.64, O = 3.73 ± 0.44 (All SW >0.957, all p>0.092, all t(44) < 1.68, all p>0.1, all Cohen's d < 0.5).
evidence: Supported by questionnaire data with statistical analysis

claim: A specific polymorphism in an olfactory receptor gene (OR4C16G > A) has been associated with uRPL.
source: Finally, it is tempting to combine the current picture of altered perception and brain responses to men's body odor in uRPL, with additional findings such as a specific polymorphism in an olfactory receptor gene (OR4C16G > A) that has been associated with uRPL (Ryu et al., 2019), and the tradition of protective isolation of women during early pregnancy evident in some tribal societies (Van Gennep, 1960), to jointly hint at a form of Bruce effect in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryu et al., 2019

claim: Some tribal societies have a tradition of protective isolation of women during early pregnancy.
source: Finally, it is tempting to combine the current picture of altered perception and brain responses to men's body odor in uRPL, with additional findings such as a specific polymorphism in an olfactory receptor gene (OR4C16G > A) that has been associated with uRPL (Ryu et al., 2019), and the tradition of protective isolation of women during early pregnancy evident in some tribal societies (Van Gennep, 1960), to jointly hint at a form of Bruce effect in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Gennep, 1960

claim: Humans may not possess a vomeronasal organ (VNO) as a functional structure.
source: The first is the VNO, namely the dedicated sensory epithelia in the rodent nasal passage that is primarily involved in social chemosignaling (Keverne, 1999). Humans may retain a VNO pit on the nasal septum (Trotier et al., 2000), but this structure is considered vestigial in the human nose (Meredith, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trotier et al., 2000 and Meredith, 2001

claim: The accessory olfactory bulb (AOB) is reported missing in the human brain.
source: Second, the rodent VNO projects to the rodent accessory olfactory bulb (AOB), a structure also reported missing in the human brain (Meisami et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meisami et al., 1998

claim: Humans functionally express vomeronasal receptors in their olfactory epithelium.
source: Although humans may lack a VNO and AOB, humans do functionally express vomeronasal receptors in their olfactory epithelium (Rodriguez et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2000

claim: The main epithelium and bulb can support social chemosignaling in rodents.
source: Although rodent social chemosignaling is primarily attributed to the VNO and AOB, the main epithelium and bulb can also support social chemosignaling (Spehr et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spehr et al., 2006

claim: Structural and functional patterns of brain organization have not been previously associated with uRPL.
source: Indeed, as far as we know, structural and functional patterns of brain organization have not been previously associated with uRPL, and this discovery was guided by our investigation of olfaction.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: Social environment may impact pregnancy loss.
source: Thus, this framework and set of findings may combine with additional results on the potential impact of social environment on pregnancy loss (Catalano et al., 2016; Catalano et al., 2018) to jointly redirect thinking on this condition, which is currently not well-understood, or managed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Catalano et al., 2016 and Catalano et al., 2018

claim: At every given measure, there were women from the uRPL group with control-like results, and women from the control group with uRPL-like results.
source: As a group, women with uRPL differed from controls, but at every given measure, there were women from the uRPL group with control-like results, and women from the control group with uRPL-like results.
evidence: Based on inference from the variability observed in the experimental data

claim: The study recruited an overall cohort of 40 women with uRPL (mean age: 35.06 ± 6.22) and 57 controls (mean age: 34.66 ± 4.24).
source: Instead, participants were available sporadically. To deal with this, we recruited an overall cohort of 40 women with uRPL (mean age: 35.06 ± 6.22), and 57 controls (mean age: 34.66 ± 4.24), and then assigned matched pairs based on uRPL availability per experiment (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data describing the participant cohort

claim: Inclusion criteria for uRPL was at least two consecutive miscarriages prior to 15 weeks, with an unknown etiology for the pregnancy loss.
source: Inclusion criteria for uRPL was at least two consecutive miscarriages prior to 15 weeks, with an unknown etiology for the pregnancy loss, despite careful medical investigation.
evidence: Describes the experimental design criteria

claim: Inclusion criteria for controls was no history of (known) pregnancy loss or abortions.
source: Inclusion criteria for controls was no history of (known) pregnancy loss or abortions.
evidence: Describes the experimental design criteria

claim: Number of pregnancies alone does not impact spouse identification performance.
source: To ask whether number of pregnancies may be associated with our results, we examined the most prominent behavioral result, namely spouse identification, and its association with number of pregnancies within each group. We observed no significant correlations (uRPL group: Spearman's Rho = 0.19, p=0.3; Control group: Spearman's Rho = −0.29, p=0.11), implying that number of pregnancies alone does not impact this result.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of experimental data

claim: Twenty-two heterosexual men (mean age 31.1 ± 6.4) donated their body-odor for the fMRI study.
source: Twenty-two heterosexual men (mean age 31.1 ± 6.4) donated their body-odor, following the standard procedures described above, with two differences: we used eight adhesive pads rather than t-shirts, for four nights rather than 2.
evidence: Describes the experimental design and participant cohort

claim: The scanner stimulus for the fMRI study contained a mix of body-odor from 20 men.
source: These pads were cut into small pieces and mixed such that the scanner stimulus contained a mix of 20 men.
evidence: Describes the experimental design

claim: Smaller olfactory bulbs are typically associated with poorer olfaction.
source: On one side, this result provides yet additional and particularly convincing evidence for an altered olfactory brain profile in uRPL. We label this as particularly convincing because volumetric differences are less susceptible to analysis strategies than are functional differences. On the other hand, whereas smaller OBs are typically associated with poorer olfaction (Buschhüter et al., 2008; Rombaux et al., 2010), here we observed smaller OBs in the group with better olfactory spouse identification (uRPL), and slightly better olfaction overall.
evidence: Supported by citations to Buschhüter et al., 2008 and Rombaux et al., 2010
